entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To resist or argue against a plan, request, decision or idea, openly but usually without refusing completely.
entries.usage: Very common in American workplaces, in meetings and email: *I want to push back on that a little* is a polite way to disagree with a manager or a colleague. Use *on* before the idea or request; *against* is common before rules, pressure or trends (*push back against the new rules*). Do not confuse it with *push back a meeting*, which means postpone it.
entries.pattern: push back on + idea / request / deadline; push back against + rules / pressure
examples: When the client asked for the full report in two days, our project lead **pushed back** and got us a week.
Several nurses **pushed back on** the new shift schedule because it left the night unit understaffed.
I'm going to **push back on** that a little. I don't think the survey shows what you're saying.

drill.sentence: The airline offered me a fifty-dollar voucher, but I {{pushed back}} and got a full refund instead.
drill.hint: resistance, as a two-word phrasal verb (not *objected* or *fought …*)

entries.related: *pushback* — the noun (*we got a lot of pushback*); *object to* — more formal; *push back (a meeting)* — a different sense, postpone.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Real agreement with a plan and active support for it from the people who must carry it out or who are affected by it.
entries.usage: A management word, common in meetings, proposals and change projects: *get buy-in from the team*, *we need buy-in from leadership*. It means commitment, not just permission, so it fits plans that depend on people's cooperation. It is usually uncountable (*get buy-in*, *a lack of buy-in*), and some people find it jargon.
entries.pattern: get / need / secure buy-in from + people; buy-in for + a plan
examples: The new expense software failed because management never got **buy-in** from the people who actually had to use it.
Before you announce the reorganization, make sure you have **buy-in** from the team leads.
We wanted to try a vegetarian Thanksgiving this year, but we couldn't get **buy-in** from Grandpa.

drill.sentence: The principal can announce a new homework policy, but it won't work without {{buy-in}} from the teachers.
drill.hint: a hyphenated business word: their agreement and commitment

entries.related: *support* — more general; *sign-off* — formal approval from someone in charge; *on board* — informal, agreeing and willing to help.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To agree with a plan or idea and be willing to support it or take part in it.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and casual work talk: *Is everyone on board?* checks for agreement before a group moves on. It sounds friendlier and less formal than *agree*, and *get someone on board* means persuade them. *Come on board* is different: it means join a company or project.
entries.pattern: be / get someone on board (with something)
examples: I love the idea of a four-day workweek, but I doubt our CEO is **on board**.
My wife wasn't **on board with** the road trip at first, but the national parks won her over.
Once the head surgeon was **on board with** the new safety checklist, the rest of the staff followed.

drill.sentence: Before you adopt a dog, make sure your roommates are {{on board}}; it's their apartment too.
drill.hint: agreement and support, as a ship image (two words)

entries.related: *buy in (to something)* — accept and commit to an idea; *go along with* — accept, often without real enthusiasm; *sign off on* — give official approval.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A single problem or condition that is serious enough to make you reject a deal, an option or a person, even if everything else is good.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about jobs, apartments, purchases and dating: *No parking is a dealbreaker for me*. It is very frequent in questions and negatives, which let you check how serious an issue is (*Is the commute a dealbreaker?*, *It's not a dealbreaker*). Also spelled *deal-breaker* or *deal breaker*.
entries.pattern: X is a dealbreaker (for someone)
examples: The salary was fine, but having to be in the office five days a week was **a dealbreaker** for me.
For a lot of renters, no laundry in the building is **a dealbreaker**.
We liked the startup's product, but the founders' refusal to share their financials was **a dealbreaker**.

drill.sentence: She liked him a lot, but he smoked, and for her that was {{a dealbreaker}}.
drill.hint: a single issue that rules him out, however good the rest is (not *a red flag* or *a no-go*)

entries.related: *a non-starter* — an idea with no chance at all; *a red flag* — a warning sign, not yet a final no; *a sticking point* — an issue still being negotiated.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To make someone answer for their results or mistakes, so that they face consequences if they fail.
entries.usage: Common in management, education, journalism and public debate, usually with *for* + the result or failure. It sounds serious and slightly formal; said to a colleague, it can sound like a threat unless you also explain what support you will give. *Hold each other accountable* is a popular team phrase for shared responsibility.
entries.pattern: hold someone accountable (for something)
examples: If each team sets clear goals, it's easier to **hold** people **accountable** at the end of the quarter.
Parents want the school board to **hold** the bus company **accountable for** the repeated delays.
My running partner and I **hold each other accountable**: if one of us skips a morning, the other one calls.

drill.sentence: If the new bridge starts cracking, who's going to {{hold the builders accountable}}?
drill.hint: consequences for the failure (four words, object in the middle; not *… responsible*)

entries.related: *hold someone responsible* — very close, more often about blame for one event; *answer for something* — face the consequences; *let someone off the hook* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To give final, official approval to a plan, document, budget or piece of work, so that it can go ahead.
entries.usage: Common in American workplaces, in speech and email: *Has legal signed off on the contract?* It implies that the person has the authority to approve and shares responsibility afterward. Americans usually add *on* before the thing approved; *sign off* alone can also mean end a broadcast, a shift or a message.
entries.pattern: sign off on + a plan / budget / design / contract
examples: We can't order the new microscope until the department chair **signs off on** the budget.
The architect won't start the construction drawings until the homeowners **sign off on** the floor plan.
The attending physician has to **sign off on** every discharge before the patient can leave.

drill.sentence: Our wedding planner needs both of us to {{sign off on}} the menu before she can order the food.
drill.hint: final approval, as a phrasal verb with *on* (not *agree on* or *approve*)

entries.related: *approve* — more formal, no particle; *green-light* — allow a project to start; *rubber-stamp* — approve without real checking, critical.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To tell someone about an idea or plan and ask for their opinion or approval before you decide or act.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and workplace chat: *Can I run something by you?* or *Let me run it by my boss*. It sounds collaborative and modest, a polite way to ask for input or to delay agreeing until you have checked with someone. The object goes in the middle (*run the idea by Sam*), and *run it past someone* means the same.
entries.pattern: run something (an idea / a plan / the numbers) by someone
examples: Before I send the offer letter, I want to **run** the numbers **by** HR.
Can I **run something by you**? I'm thinking of asking my landlord if I can paint the bedroom.
The teacher **ran** the field trip plan **by** the principal before telling the parents.

drill.sentence: That sounds like a good deal, but let me {{run it by}} my wife before I say yes.
drill.hint: an informal check of her opinion (three words ending in *by*; not *check it with*)

entries.related: *check with someone* — ask for approval or facts; *bounce an idea off someone* — test an idea in conversation; *consult* — formal, ask an expert.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To ask someone who knows a lot about a subject for ideas, information or advice, usually in an informal conversation.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and networking messages: *Could I pick your brain about grad school?* It is friendly and flattering because it treats the other person as an expert, but some busy people are tired of hearing it. In a first email to a senior stranger, *I'd love your advice on …* plus one specific question is safer.
entries.pattern: pick someone's brain (about / on something)
examples: You've hired a lot of engineers. Could I **pick your brain** about running technical interviews?
My uncle is a contractor, so I **picked his brain** before we hired anyone to redo the kitchen.
The new residents love **picking her brain** about difficult diagnoses during night shifts.

drill.sentence: Since you've run two marathons, can I {{pick your brain}} about training plans over coffee sometime?
drill.hint: informal request for your expert advice (an idiom with a body part)

entries.related: *ask someone's advice* — neutral and safe in any setting; *tap someone's expertise* — more formal; *bounce ideas off someone* — test your own ideas on them.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A rough estimate that gives an idea of the size of a number, without claiming to be exact.
entries.usage: Very common in American business talk when someone needs a number quickly: *Can you give me a ballpark figure?* It signals that both sides accept the number is approximate, so it is a low-pressure way to ask for an estimate. *In the ballpark* means close to the right number, and *ballpark* is also a verb (*Can you ballpark it?*).
entries.pattern: give someone a ballpark figure / number / estimate; in the ballpark (of)
examples: I know it's early, but can you give me **a ballpark figure** for the kitchen renovation?
The vendor wouldn't commit to a price, but his **ballpark figure** was about twenty thousand dollars.
Just **a ballpark figure** is fine: are we talking about hundreds of volunteers or thousands?

drill.sentence: I don't need an exact quote yet, just {{a ballpark figure}} so I know whether we can afford it.
drill.hint: how much, roughly (three words, a baseball image; the last word is not *number* or *estimate*)

entries.related: *a rough estimate* — neutral, fine in writing; *a guesstimate* — informal, half guess and half estimate; *in the ballpark* — close to the right amount.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To make sure that people do not expect more than you can realistically deliver, usually by being clear early about limits, risks or timelines.
entries.usage: Common in project management, customer service, medicine and parenting talk: *We need to manage the client's expectations*. Said about someone else, it can sound manipulative, so in direct conversation people say *I want to be realistic with you about …* instead. It often appears as *manage someone's expectations* or the noun *expectation management*.
entries.pattern: manage (someone's) expectations (about something)
examples: The surgeon was careful to **manage** the family's **expectations**: the operation would help him, but it wouldn't cure him.
We're **managing expectations** with the client by promising a prototype, not a finished product.
I tried to **manage** my kids' **expectations** by telling them the cabin had no Wi-Fi.

drill.sentence: Before the season started, the new coach tried to {{manage expectations}}, saying the team was still rebuilding.
drill.hint: realistic hopes, as a verb + noun (not *lower*, *temper* or *dampen*)

entries.related: *temper expectations* — make them more moderate; *lower the bar* — accept a lower standard; *underpromise and overdeliver* — promise little, then deliver more.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To accept full responsibility for a task, problem or result, including making sure it gets done or fixed.
entries.usage: A popular phrase in management and performance reviews: *I'd like you to take ownership of the onboarding process*. It praises initiative, but managers also use it as a polite demand, and it can sound like corporate jargon. In plain speech, *be in charge of* or *take responsibility for* says the same.
entries.pattern: take (full) ownership of + a task / project / mistake
examples: Maria **took ownership of** the patient-safety project and turned it into a hospital-wide program.
Instead of blaming the intern, the team lead **took ownership of** the mistake in front of the client.
At sixteen, our son started **taking ownership of** his own schedule, which was a huge relief.

drill.sentence: Nobody has {{taken ownership of}} the website redesign, which is why it keeps falling through the cracks.
drill.hint: full responsibility, in management jargon (three words ending in *of*; not *charge*)

entries.related: *take charge of* — take control and lead; *own* — very informal jargon (*Can you own this?*); *pass the buck* — the opposite, push responsibility onto others.

entries.label: work jargon
entries.meaning: To be unable to continue your work until someone else does something or another problem is solved.
entries.usage: Common in tech companies, startups and research teams, in stand-ups, chat and status updates: *I'm blocked on the access request*. The thing after *on* is what you are waiting for, and the noun *a blocker* names it. Outside tech-style workplaces it can sound like jargon, so *I'm waiting on …* or *I can't continue until …* is safer.
entries.pattern: be blocked on + a task / approval / person; a blocker
examples: I'm **blocked on** the database migration until IT gives me admin access.
Half the team was **blocked on** legal review, so the launch slipped a week.
We're **blocked on** ethics approval, so we can't start recruiting participants yet.

drill.sentence: In today's stand-up, Priya said she was {{blocked on}} the design files and couldn't start coding yet.
drill.hint: unable to continue until she gets them (not *stuck* or *waiting*)

entries.related: *be stuck on* — unable to solve something yourself; *be waiting on* — plainer, less jargon; *unblock someone* — remove what stops them.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To quickly check that something is roughly correct or makes sense, to catch obvious errors before you rely on it.
entries.usage: Common among engineers, scientists, analysts and doctors, in speech and chat: *Can you sanity-check these numbers?* It asks for a light, fast check, not a full review, so it is a low-pressure way to ask a colleague for help. Some company style guides avoid it because it refers to mental health and suggest *quick check* or *confidence check* instead.
entries.pattern: sanity-check + numbers / results / a plan; do a sanity check (on something)
examples: Before I submit the budget, could you **sanity-check** the totals? I've been staring at them all day.
I always ask a friend to **sanity-check** my cover letters for anything that sounds weird.
The pharmacist **sanity-checked** the dose and called the doctor because it looked ten times too high.

drill.sentence: Can you {{sanity-check}} my travel plans? I'm not sure four cities in five days is realistic.
drill.hint: a quick test for obvious nonsense (hyphenated; not *double-…* or *look over*)

entries.related: *double-check* — check again carefully; *look over* — read through quickly; *proofread* — check a text for language errors.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A decision that depends on someone's own judgment and experience, because no clear rule or data settles it.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports, in medicine and in everyday talk. It is often used to explain or defend a decision (*I made a judgment call*) or to hand a decision to someone else (*That's your judgment call*). American spelling is *judgment*; British writers often use *judgement*.
entries.pattern: make a judgment call; it's a judgment call (whether …)
examples: There's no protocol for a case like this, so whether to operate tonight is **a judgment call**.
The referee made **a judgment call**, and the replays suggest he got it right.
Whether to wake the baby for a feeding is **a judgment call**, so trust your instincts.

drill.sentence: Whether to cancel the picnic with a forty percent chance of rain is really {{a judgment call}}.
drill.hint: no rule settles it, so it's up to someone's good sense (not *a toss-up* or *a tough …*)

entries.related: *a toss-up* — two options are equally likely or good; *at your discretion* — formal, you may decide; *a gray area* — a situation where the rules are unclear.

entries.label: adjective phrase
entries.meaning: To be honest and open about something from the beginning, especially something the other person might not like.
entries.usage: Common in negotiation, hiring, dating and everyday conversation: *I want to be upfront about my schedule*. Saying *I'll be upfront with you* before bad news signals honesty and respect. Use *with* before the person and *about* before the topic; it is also spelled *up front*.
entries.pattern: be upfront (with someone) about something
examples: I want to be **upfront** about the budget: we can't match your current salary.
She was **upfront** with the buyers about the leaky basement, and they still made an offer.
If you're seeing other people, just be **upfront about** it.

drill.sentence: In the interview, I was {{upfront}} about needing to leave at three every day to pick up my kids.
drill.hint: hiding nothing from the start (one word; not *honest*, *open*, *frank*, *candid* or *transparent*)

entries.related: *straightforward* — direct and easy to understand; *candid* — frank, sometimes surprisingly so; *beat around the bush* — the opposite, avoid saying it directly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To give a particular impression to other people, often one you did not intend.
entries.usage: Very common in feedback and everyday talk, especially about tone: *Your email came across as a bit harsh*. It is a soft way to criticize, because it describes the effect on others rather than the person's intent. Use *as* + adjective or noun (*came across as rude*, *as a know-it-all*); without *as*, you can say *come across well* or *badly*.
entries.pattern: come across as + adjective / noun (to someone)
examples: I don't think you meant it that way, but your comment in the meeting **came across as** dismissive.
He can **come across as** arrogant, but he's actually really shy.
In her video interview, the candidate **came across as** calm and well prepared.

drill.sentence: My text was supposed to be a joke, but it {{came across as}} passive-aggressive.
drill.hint: how it was perceived (three words ending in *as*; not *sounded*, *read as* or the *off* version)

entries.related: *seem* — more general; *strike someone as* — give someone an impression (*He struck me as honest*); *come off as* — very close, a bit more informal.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An idea, plan or proposal that has no chance of being accepted or of succeeding, so it is not worth discussing.
entries.usage: Common in negotiations, politics and office talk: *A pay cut is a non-starter for the union*. It is blunt but not rude, a firm way to rule something out early. It is usually said about proposals; compare *a dealbreaker*, which is one issue that makes you reject a whole deal.
entries.pattern: X is a non-starter (for someone)
examples: A price increase this quarter is **a non-starter**; we'd lose our biggest customer.
For my parents, moving into assisted living was **a non-starter**, so we hired a caregiver instead.
The proposal to start school at seven was **a non-starter** with parents.

drill.sentence: Asking my boss for a three-month vacation is {{a non-starter}}, but maybe I can get two extra weeks.
drill.hint: zero chance of approval (hyphenated noun; not *out of the question* or *a no-go*)

entries.related: *out of the question* — impossible, not allowed; *a dealbreaker* — one issue that makes you reject a deal; *dead on arrival* — a proposal that fails immediately.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Criticism given in a specific, helpful way so that the person can improve, rather than only to point out what is wrong.
entries.usage: Standard in schools, workplaces and performance reviews: *give*, *get* or *ask for constructive feedback*. Good constructive feedback names a specific behavior and suggests a change, so the phrase sounds supportive and professional. Because people sometimes use it as a polite label for harsh criticism, it can also sound ironic (*Thanks for the "constructive" feedback*).
entries.pattern: give / get / ask for constructive feedback (on something)
examples: My advisor's **constructive feedback** on my first draft was tough to hear, but it made the proposal much stronger.
The coach gave each player some **constructive feedback** after the game instead of just yelling.
Our new manager asked us for **constructive feedback** on how she runs meetings.

drill.sentence: Instead of just saying the essay was bad, the teacher gave {{constructive feedback}} on how to fix the argument.
drill.hint: the standard two-word phrase for criticism meant to help (the second word is not *criticism*)

mistake.wrong: She gave me some constructive feedbacks on my talk.
mistake.right: She gave me some constructive feedback on my talk.
mistake.why: *Feedback* is uncountable, so it has no plural *-s* and no *a*; for one comment, say *a piece of feedback*.

entries.related: *criticism* — can be negative or harsh; *input* — ideas or opinions, not necessarily critical; *a critique* — a detailed, formal evaluation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To compromise with someone, with each side giving up part of what it wants in order to reach an agreement.
entries.usage: Common in negotiations, relationships and everyday bargaining: *I can't do five hundred, but I'll meet you halfway*. It sounds cooperative and fair, so it is a friendly way to propose a compromise. The literal sense, meeting at a place between two homes or cities, is also common, and context makes the meaning clear.
entries.pattern: meet someone halfway (on something); meet each other halfway
examples: The client wanted a fifty percent discount, and we finally **met them halfway** at twenty-five.
My teenager wanted a midnight curfew and I wanted ten, so we **met each other halfway** at eleven.
The seller wouldn't drop the price, but she **met us halfway** by throwing in the snow tires.

drill.sentence: My sister wanted to drive straight through, and I wanted to stop for two nights, so we {{met each other halfway}} and stopped for one.
drill.hint: a compromise from both sides (three words; not *compromised*, *split the difference* or *met in the middle*)

entries.related: *split the difference* — agree on a number exactly between two offers; *compromise* — more general and neutral; *give and take* — the willingness of both sides to make concessions.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A particular issue that people cannot agree on and that stops a negotiation or discussion from reaching agreement.
entries.usage: Common in news reports on negotiations and in business talk: *The main sticking point is the price*. It is neutral and descriptive, so it is a diplomatic way to name a conflict without blaming anyone. It usually appears as *the (main / biggest) sticking point is …* or *remains a sticking point*.
entries.pattern: the main / biggest sticking point (in something); remain a sticking point
examples: Health insurance for part-time staff was the main **sticking point** in the contract talks.
We agreed on almost everything in the divorce; the only **sticking point** was the dog.
Authorship order became **a sticking point** between the two labs, and the paper sat unfinished for months.

drill.sentence: The neighbors agree the old fence has to go, but who pays for the new one is still {{a sticking point}}.
drill.hint: where the talks get stuck (not *a bone of contention* or *an issue*)

entries.related: *a bone of contention* — a topic people keep arguing about, often for a long time; *a dealbreaker* — an issue that ends the deal; *an impasse* — formal, a complete deadlock.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To give people tasks or roles that use their best skills, or to act in a way that uses your own best abilities.
entries.usage: Common in management, coaching and career advice: *A good manager plays to people's strengths*. It sounds positive and supportive, so it is a tactful way to explain why someone is not given a certain task. The possessive changes (*play to her strengths*, *play to our strengths*), and *strengths* is usually plural.
entries.pattern: play to someone's / your (own) strengths
examples: Jamal is great with clients, so let's **play to his strengths** and have him lead the pitch.
The coach **played to the team's strengths**: short passes and fast breaks instead of long shots.
In your cover letter, **play to your strengths** instead of apologizing for the gap in your résumé.

drill.sentence: She's a brilliant writer but a nervous speaker, so the team {{played to her strengths}} and had her write the script.
drill.hint: an idiom about using someone's best skills

entries.related: *make the most of someone's talents* — plainer; *shore up weaknesses* — improve weak areas, the opposite focus; *a good fit* — suited to a role.

entries.label: work jargon
entries.meaning: A very small, picky comment in a code review or document review, usually about style or wording rather than a real problem.
entries.usage: Common in American software teams and increasingly in research groups; reviewers often start a comment with *nit:* to signal that it is optional. It is a polite, self-aware way to point out something minor without blocking approval. It comes from *nitpick*; outside these settings, say *a minor point* or *a small suggestion*.
entries.pattern: a (small) nit; "nit:" + comment; just nits
examples: Looks good to me! Just a couple of **nits** about spacing, but nothing that blocks merging.
My editor's comments were mostly **nits**: commas, word choice and one misspelled name.
Sorry, small **nit**: the two charts use slightly different shades of blue.

drill.sentence: Approved! I left one {{nit}} about a typo in a comment, but feel free to ignore it.
drill.hint: a tiny, optional remark (three-letter code-review slang)

entries.related: *nitpick* — a picky criticism, or to make one, often negative; *a blocker* — a problem that must be fixed before approval; *a minor point* — neutral, any setting.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A concrete result, such as a report, product or piece of software, that a project has promised to produce by a certain date.
entries.usage: Standard in project management, consulting, grants and contracts, usually in the plural: *the deliverables for phase one*. It sounds formal and businesslike; in conversation people often just name the thing (*the report*, *the app*). Deliverables are usually tied to deadlines or payments, so missing one is serious.
entries.pattern: the deliverables (for a project / phase); a key deliverable
examples: The first **deliverable** is a short report on how patients use the clinic's app.
Our grant has four **deliverables**, and the funder checks each one at the end of the year.
Before we sign, let's agree on the **deliverables** and when each one is due.

drill.sentence: The contract lists three {{deliverables}}: a website, a logo and a one-page brand guide.
drill.hint: what the agency must hand over (project-management word; not *items* or *outputs*)

entries.related: *an action item* — a task someone agreed to do after a meeting; *a milestone* — a planned point of progress; *an output* — a more general word for a result.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The tasks, problems or gains that are easiest to achieve, so they are usually dealt with first.
entries.usage: Very common in business, policy and project talk: *Let's go after the low-hanging fruit first*. It is a famous cliché, so many people mock it as corporate jargon; *the easy wins* or *the quick fixes* sound fresher. It can also sound dismissive, as if someone only did the easy part.
entries.pattern: go after / pick / grab the low-hanging fruit
examples: Before we redesign the whole app, let's grab the **low-hanging fruit**: the broken links and the typos on the home page.
Most cities have already picked the **low-hanging fruit** in recycling; the next gains will be much harder.
In the clinic, the **low-hanging fruit** was cutting the wait for lab results from three days to one.

drill.sentence: If you want to cut your monthly costs, canceling subscriptions you never use is the {{low-hanging fruit}}.
drill.hint: the easiest gains to grab first (a cliché; not *the easy win* or *quick wins*)

entries.related: *a quick win* — an easy early success; *the easy part* — plain and neutral; *a heavy lift* — the opposite, a hard task.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person or group that is affected by a project or decision, or has an interest in it, and therefore expects to be consulted.
entries.usage: Standard in management, public planning, health care and grant writing: *We need to involve all the key stakeholders*. It is very frequent in the plural and sounds official, so in casual speech people often say *everyone involved*. Some people find it overused jargon, especially in phrases like *stakeholder engagement*.
entries.pattern: (key / major) stakeholders; consult / involve / engage stakeholders
examples: Before closing the clinic, the hospital met with patients, staff and other **stakeholders**.
Parents, teachers and students are all **stakeholders** in the new school schedule.
Can you send the draft to the main **stakeholders** and ask for comments by Friday?

drill.sentence: The park redesign affects dog owners, parents, local businesses and other {{stakeholders}}, so the city held a public meeting.
drill.hint: those with an interest in the outcome (business word; not *groups* or *parties*)

entries.related: *shareholder* — owns shares in a company, a narrower word; *interested parties* — formal, often legal; *the end users* — the people who will use a product.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To find opinions, interests or goals that two sides share, even though they disagree about other things.
entries.usage: Common in negotiation, family discussions and news reports: *The two sides struggled to find common ground*. It is warm and constructive, a good way to suggest starting from what people agree on. Also *look for*, *seek* or *search for common ground*, and *there's little common ground between …*.
entries.pattern: find / look for / seek common ground (with someone) (on something)
examples: My dad and I disagree about almost everything, but we **found common ground** in our love of baseball.
The new manager's first job was to **find common ground** between sales and engineering.
After weeks of talks, the city and the bus drivers' union finally **found common ground** on overtime pay.

drill.sentence: Even when you strongly disagree with a coworker, try to {{find common ground}} before arguing about the details.
drill.hint: shared views as a starting point (three words; not *compromise*; not *a middle …*)

entries.related: *a middle ground* — a compromise position between two extremes; *see eye to eye* — agree completely; *meet someone halfway* — each side gives up part of what it wants.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A position, choice or solution between two extremes that both sides can accept.
entries.usage: Common in discussion and negotiation: *Is there a middle ground between working from home and five days in the office?* It sounds balanced and reasonable, and it usually follows *there is*, *find* or *look for*. Note the difference from *common ground*: *common ground* means opinions people already share, while *a middle ground* is a compromise position.
entries.pattern: find / look for a middle ground (between A and B); there's a middle ground
examples: The team wanted daily meetings and the manager wanted none, so we found **a middle ground**: twice a week.
Is there **a middle ground** between letting kids have phones all day and banning them completely?
The new parking rules are **a middle ground** between what residents and shop owners wanted.

drill.sentence: My son wants to quit piano, and I want him to practice every day. There has to be {{a middle ground}}.
drill.hint: a position between the two extremes (three words; not *a compromise* or *a happy medium*)

entries.related: *a happy medium* — a satisfying balance between two extremes; *a compromise* — an agreement in which both sides give something up; *common ground* — shared views.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A new offer made in reply to someone else's offer, usually with a different price or different conditions.
entries.usage: Common in salary negotiations, house buying and business deals: *make*, *accept* or *reject a counteroffer*. In job talk it also means an offer from your current employer to keep you after you get another job offer. Americans usually write it as one word, and *counter* alone works as a verb (*The buyers countered with a lower offer*).
entries.pattern: make / accept / reject a counteroffer
examples: The sellers rejected our first offer but came back with **a counteroffer** only five thousand dollars higher.
When she told her boss she was leaving, the company made **a counteroffer** with a bigger salary and a new title.
The publisher's **counteroffer** gave the author a smaller advance but a bigger share of the royalties.

drill.sentence: Don't just accept the first salary they offer; it's normal to make {{a counteroffer}}.
drill.hint: your own reply to their number (one word after *a*; not *a counter* or *a counterproposal*)

entries.related: *a counterproposal* — a different plan offered in reply, not only a price; *haggle* — argue about a price, informal; *a lowball offer* — an offer far below the value.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To offer someone much less money than something is really worth, often hoping they will accept anyway.
entries.usage: Common in American speech about salaries, cars, houses and online sales: *They tried to lowball me*. It is critical, so people use it about the other side's offer, not their own, unless they are joking. It also works as an adjective (*a lowball offer*) and can mean giving a deliberately low estimate (*lowball the cost*).
entries.pattern: lowball someone (on something); a lowball offer
examples: The dealer tried to **lowball** me on my trade-in, so I sold the car privately.
I think they **lowballed** her: the salary is about twenty percent below what others in her role make.
Expect buyers on Facebook Marketplace to **lowball** you, so list the couch a little higher than you want.

drill.sentence: The buyer offered half our asking price; he was obviously trying to {{lowball}} us.
drill.hint: a far-too-low offer, as an informal verb (not *cheat*)

entries.related: *rip someone off* — cheat someone, usually by charging too much; *haggle* — argue about a price; *a counteroffer* — a reply to an offer.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To have something that gives you power in a negotiation or relationship, so the other side has to take your demands seriously.
entries.usage: Common in business, negotiation and the news: *Having another offer gives you leverage*. Use *over* for the other person and *in* for the situation (*leverage in the talks*); *use something as leverage* is also common. Most Americans say LEV-er-ij; LEE-ver-ij, the usual British form, is also heard in the US.
entries.pattern: have / gain / lose leverage (over someone / in something); use something as leverage
examples: Because she had another job offer, she **had** a lot of **leverage** in the salary talks.
The landlord knows we can't find another apartment before school starts, so he **has leverage over** us.
Our best engineer **has leverage**: if she leaves, the whole project stalls.

drill.sentence: Our only supplier knows we can't switch to anyone else, so they {{have leverage over}} us.
drill.hint: bargaining power (three words; not *the upper hand*, *power over* or *control over*)

entries.related: *bargaining power* — plainer, same idea; *have the upper hand* — have an advantage in any contest; *have someone over a barrel* — informal, they have no choice.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that one side can offer, trade or threaten to hold back in a negotiation to get what it wants.
entries.usage: Common in news about negotiations and business, and in jokes about family life. It often suggests that people or important issues are being used cynically (*They're using the kids as a bargaining chip*). Typical patterns are *use something as a bargaining chip* and *become a bargaining chip*.
entries.pattern: use something / someone as a bargaining chip
examples: The company used its new factory as **a bargaining chip** to get tax breaks from the state.
My little brother uses his good grades as **a bargaining chip** for more screen time.
In the talks, vacation days became **a bargaining chip**: the union gave some up in exchange for higher pay.

drill.sentence: My roommate uses the fact that she owns the TV as {{a bargaining chip}} whenever we argue about chores.
drill.hint: a trading piece in negotiations, from gambling (not *leverage* or *a pawn*)

entries.related: *leverage* — the power you have, not the thing you trade; *a pawn* — a person used by others for their own goals; *a trade-off* — giving up one thing to get another.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Fixed and not open to discussion or change, because it is a firm requirement or limit.
entries.usage: Common in negotiations, job ads, parenting and lifestyle talk: *Safety rules are non-negotiable*. It sounds firm and final, so with a colleague *This is really important to me* can sound less rigid. It works after a verb (*is non-negotiable*), before a noun (*a non-negotiable deadline*) and as a plural noun (*my non-negotiables*).
entries.pattern: X is non-negotiable; a non-negotiable deadline / condition / requirement
examples: Hand washing between patients is **non-negotiable**, no matter how busy the ward gets.
Bedtime at eight is **non-negotiable** on school nights, even if they beg.
We can move the launch date, but the security review is **non-negotiable**.

drill.sentence: You can pick the music and the snacks, but wearing a seatbelt in my car is {{non-negotiable}}.
drill.hint: fixed, with no debate allowed (hyphenated adjective; not *mandatory* or *required*)

entries.related: *a red line* — a limit that must not be crossed, often with consequences; *set in stone* — fixed and impossible to change; *flexible* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A small amount of freedom to change a plan, a price, a deadline or the meaning of what was said.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and business: *Is there any wiggle room on the price?* is a polite, casual way to ask whether a number can change. It also describes vague wording that lets someone escape a commitment later. British speakers more often say *wriggle room* or *room for manoeuvre*.
entries.pattern: (some / any / a little) wiggle room on / in something
examples: The asking price is firm, but there might be some **wiggle room** on the closing date.
The school's dress code leaves a lot of **wiggle room**: "appropriate clothing" could mean almost anything.
The deadline is Friday at five, and there's no **wiggle room**.

drill.sentence: The contract says payment within thirty days, but is there any {{wiggle room}} if we're a little late?
drill.hint: slight freedom to adjust (informal; not *flexibility* or *leeway*)

entries.related: *leeway* — freedom to act, neutral; *flexibility* — more formal; *breathing room* — extra time or space to relax a little.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To add something extra to an offer to make it more attractive, so the other side is more likely to accept.
entries.usage: Common in business news, sales and everyday bargaining: *To sweeten the deal, they threw in free delivery*. The extra is usually money, a perk or a free item, and the phrase often starts a sentence as *To sweeten the deal, …*. *Sweeten the offer* and *sweeten the pot* are close variants.
entries.pattern: sweeten the deal (with something / by doing something)
examples: To **sweeten the deal**, the startup offered her stock options on top of the salary.
The seller **sweetened the deal** by including the washer and dryer.
Can you cover my Sunday shift? I'll **sweeten the deal** by buying you lunch all week.

drill.sentence: The clinic couldn't match the hospital's salary, so it {{sweetened the deal}} with extra vacation and a four-day week.
drill.hint: extras to make the offer tempting (not *…the offer* or *…the pot*)

entries.related: *throw in* — add something for free; *up the ante* — raise the stakes or the demands; *a perk* — an extra benefit of a job.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To end a negotiation and refuse the deal because the terms are not acceptable.
entries.usage: Common in business, house buying and negotiation advice: *Be ready to walk away*. Being willing to walk away is often described as your main source of power in a negotiation. Use *from* + the deal or the talks; *walk away with* is different and means win or leave with something (*walk away with first prize*).
entries.pattern: walk away (from a deal / the table / the talks)
examples: When the buyer demanded a ten-thousand-dollar discount after the inspection, we **walked away**.
The software company **walked away from** the merger when the other side's debts came to light.
The best advice I got about buying a car: always be ready to **walk away**.

drill.sentence: If the moving company won't put the price in writing, we should just {{walk away}} and call someone else.
drill.hint: ending the negotiation on purpose (two words; not *back out*, *pull out* or *pass*)

entries.related: *back out (of something)* — withdraw from something already agreed; *pull out* — withdraw, often from a deal or a race; *a dealbreaker* — the issue that makes you leave.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: No longer being offered, considered or discussed as an option.
entries.usage: Common in negotiations, politics and everyday planning: *A pay cut is off the table*. Saying it about your own option is a firm way to close it, while *nothing is off the table* means every option is still possible. The opposite is *on the table* (*Everything's on the table*), and you can also *take something off the table*.
entries.pattern: be off the table; take something off the table
examples: After the board meeting, layoffs are **off the table**, at least for this year.
With the baby due in March, a big trip this spring is **off the table**.
The seller took the furniture **off the table** once we asked for a lower price.

drill.sentence: We've decided that moving to a new city is {{off the table}} until the kids finish high school.
drill.hint: dropped as an option (three words with *the*; not *out of the question* or *not an option*)

entries.related: *on the table* — being offered or discussed; *out of the question* — impossible or not allowed; *a non-starter* — an idea with no chance from the start.

entries.label: verb phrase
entries.meaning: To accept the general idea or basic terms of something, while the details still need to be discussed or confirmed.
entries.usage: Common in business, legal and news language: *The two companies have agreed in principle to merge*. It signals real progress but no final commitment, so people use it to say yes cautiously. Also *an agreement in principle*; do not write *principal*, which means main or the head of a school.
entries.pattern: agree in principle (to do something / on something / with something)
examples: The landlord **agreed in principle** to let us sublet, but he wants to meet the new tenant first.
The two hospitals have **agreed in principle** to share an emergency department.
I **agree in principle** with a four-day week, but I don't see how it would work for a restaurant.

drill.sentence: My brother and I {{agreed in principle}} to split the cost of Mom's new hearing aids, but we haven't talked numbers yet.
drill.hint: said yes to the general idea only (three words)

mistake.wrong: We agreed in principal to the new schedule.
mistake.right: We agreed in principle to the new schedule.
mistake.why: *Principle* means a basic idea or rule; *principal* means main or the head of a school.

entries.related: *a handshake deal* — an informal agreement without a written contract; *sign off on* — give final approval; *a memorandum of understanding* — a formal, non-binding agreement.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To admit in a discussion that the other person is right about one particular thing, without agreeing with everything they say.
entries.usage: Common in debates, meetings and negotiations, and a respectful way to disagree: *I'll concede that point, but …*. It shows fairness and often comes right before *but* and your main argument. Variants are *concede the point* and *I'll concede that*; in casual speech, *Fair point* or *You've got a point* is more natural.
entries.pattern: concede a / the / that point (to someone); I'll concede that …, but …
examples: I'll **concede the point** about cost, but the cheaper software would take months to learn.
After an hour of arguing, my brother finally **conceded the point**: the movie was too long.
Good negotiators **concede small points** early to build trust for the bigger ones.

drill.sentence: OK, I'll {{concede that point}}: the hotel is cheaper. But it's an hour from the beach.
drill.hint: acknowledging you win on this one thing (three words; not *grant you that*, *give you that* or *admit that*)

entries.related: *grant* — accept as true for the argument (*I'll grant you that*); *fair point* — casual spoken agreement; *stand your ground* — the opposite, refuse to give in.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A limit that you will not let anyone cross in a negotiation or relationship, because crossing it would end the deal or bring serious consequences.
entries.usage: Common in diplomacy, business, labor talks and talk about personal boundaries: *Mandatory overtime is a red line for us*. It is stronger than *non-negotiable*, since it suggests that crossing it will trigger a serious response. The usual verbs are *draw*, *set* and *cross*.
entries.pattern: draw / set / cross a red line; X is a red line (for someone)
examples: For the pilots, any cut to their rest time between flights was **a red line**.
I'm flexible about most things in a roommate, but smoking indoors is **a red line**.
The CEO said selling customer data was **a red line** the company would never cross.

drill.sentence: We can negotiate salary and start date, but working weekends is {{a red line}} for me.
drill.hint: an uncrossable limit (two words after *a*; not *a dealbreaker* or *a hard no*)

entries.related: *a dealbreaker* — one issue that makes you reject a deal; *non-negotiable* — not open to discussion; *draw the line at* — refuse to go beyond a limit.

entries.label: work jargon
entries.meaning: To remove whatever is stopping someone from continuing their work, such as a missing decision, approval or piece of information.
entries.usage: Common in tech companies and project teams, in stand-ups and chat: *Can you unblock me on the access request?* Managers often describe their main job as unblocking their team. Outside these workplaces it sounds like jargon, and on social media it means letting a blocked person contact you again.
entries.pattern: unblock someone (on something); unblock a task
examples: Approving that one access request would **unblock** three people on my team.
My main job as a manager is to **unblock** the team, not to tell them how to write code.
Once legal approved the new wording, it **unblocked** the marketing team, and the campaign went out the next day.

drill.sentence: Can you send me the login details? That would {{unblock}} me, and I could finish the report today.
drill.hint: removal of whatever stops my work (a tech-office verb)

entries.related: *be blocked on* — be unable to continue; *free someone up* — give someone time for other work; *clear the way* — remove obstacles in general.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To pass a problem or complaint to someone with more authority because it cannot be solved at the current level.
entries.usage: Common in customer service, IT, hospitals and corporate work: *If it's not fixed by Friday, I'll escalate it*. Said to the person you are dealing with, it can sound like a threat, so with colleagues it is safer to say *I'd like to get my manager's input*. Use *to* + the person or level; without an object, *escalate* usually means become more serious (*the argument escalated*).
entries.pattern: escalate something (to someone / to a higher level)
examples: The support agent couldn't fix my refund, so she **escalated** it to her supervisor.
If a patient's oxygen drops below ninety percent, the nurse should **escalate** her concerns to the doctor on call.
Before you **escalate** this to HR, have you tried talking to him directly?

drill.sentence: I've complained to the building manager three times about the leak; if nothing changes, I'll {{escalate}} it to the owner.
drill.hint: a formal move up the chain of authority (not *take*, *bring* or *report*)

entries.related: *take it up with* — raise a complaint with a person; *go over someone's head* — go to their boss without asking them first; *de-escalate* — make a conflict calmer.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The person who is responsible for one task, project or contact, so that others know whom to go to with questions.
entries.usage: Common in American workplaces, schools and organizations: *Dana is our point person for the move*. It sounds practical and clear, and naming one point person avoids confusion about who decides. Use *for* + the task or *on* + the project; *point of contact* means almost the same and is more formal.
entries.pattern: the point person for / on something
examples: Who's the **point person** for the conference? I have a question about hotel reimbursements.
For the school play, one parent is the **point person** for costumes and another for snacks.
In the ICU, the charge nurse is the **point person** for any problems during the night shift.

drill.sentence: I'll be traveling next week, so Jordan will be the {{point person}} for anything urgent about the move.
drill.hint: the one to go to (not *contact* or *go-to*)

entries.related: *point of contact* — more formal, often in emails; *a go-to person* — someone you rely on for help; *the owner* — jargon, the person responsible for a task.

entries.label: adjective phrase
entries.meaning: Having so many tasks or responsibilities that you cannot do any of them well, or having too few people or resources for the work.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, about people, teams and budgets: *Our nurses are stretched thin*. It is a sympathetic way to explain why something is slow or late without blaming anyone. It is often used with *too* or *really* (*stretched too thin*), and *spread thin* means almost the same.
entries.pattern: be / feel stretched (too) thin
examples: With two nurses out sick, the whole night shift was **stretched thin**.
I'd love to help with the fundraiser, but I'm **stretched** pretty **thin** right now.
The startup's engineers were **stretched too thin** to fix bugs and build new features at the same time.

drill.sentence: Between a new baby, a full-time job and night classes, she's been {{stretched thin}} for months.
drill.hint: with too many demands to handle well (not *spread …* or *swamped*)

entries.related: *spread thin* — almost the same; *swamped* — very busy right now; *burned out* — exhausted after too much stress for too long.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The gradual, uncontrolled growth of a project's goals or requirements after it has started, usually without extra time or money.
entries.usage: Standard in project management, software, consulting and research: *We need to watch out for scope creep*. It is a critical term, so naming it can be a polite way to refuse extra requests. It is uncountable (*a lot of scope creep*), and in software *feature creep* is a close variant.
entries.pattern: (a lot of / avoid / prevent) scope creep
examples: The app was supposed to take three months, but **scope creep** turned it into a year.
What started as a new bathroom became a whole-house renovation: classic **scope creep**.
My advisor warned that adding a third aim to the thesis would be pure **scope creep**.

drill.sentence: The client keeps adding "small" features without changing the deadline. That's {{scope creep}}, and we need to say something.
drill.hint: a project's goals growing bit by bit, out of control (not *feature …*)

entries.related: *feature creep* — adding more and more features to a product; *mission creep* — a mission's goals growing beyond the original plan; *moving the goalposts* — changing the targets unfairly.

entries.label: business saying
entries.meaning: To promise less than you expect to achieve, so that the final result is better than people expected.
entries.usage: A popular piece of business and career advice, in speech and in management books: *Always underpromise and overdeliver*. It is a way of managing expectations, and many people hear it as a cliché. Critics say that doing it all the time looks like padding your estimates, so use it with some care.
entries.pattern: underpromise and overdeliver (on something)
examples: Tell the client four weeks, even if you think it'll take three. **Underpromise and overdeliver**.
Our contractor likes to **underpromise and overdeliver**, so he always quotes a longer schedule.
The restaurant **underpromised and overdelivered**: they said an hour, and we sat down in twenty minutes.

drill.sentence: My first boss taught me a simple rule: {{underpromise and overdeliver}}, so people are pleasantly surprised.
drill.hint: a three-word saying about modest promises and better results

entries.related: *manage expectations* — keep people's hopes realistic; *pad an estimate* — add extra time or money to be safe; *overpromise* — the opposite, promise too much.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To decide that something is less important than before, so it gets less time, money or attention.
entries.usage: Common in corporate, tech and project planning language: *We're deprioritizing the mobile app this quarter*. It is a soft, neutral way to say that work will not happen soon, and often a polite way to say no. Outside office settings it sounds like jargon, and people more often say *put something on the back burner*.
entries.pattern: deprioritize + a project / feature / task (in favor of something)
examples: We've **deprioritized** the redesign so we can focus on fixing the checkout bugs.
Since the baby came, we've **deprioritized** pretty much everything except sleep.
The school board **deprioritized** the new gym in favor of repairing the leaking roof.

drill.sentence: Because of budget cuts, the hospital {{deprioritized}} the new parking garage and spent the money on staff.
drill.hint: decided it mattered less for now (not *postponed*, *delayed* or *shelved*)

entries.related: *put on the back burner* — informal, set aside for later; *shelve* — stop working on a plan, maybe for good; *prioritize* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To make a noticeable, measurable difference to a result, such as sales, public opinion or performance.
entries.usage: Common in American business, marketing and media talk, often in the negative: *A small discount won't move the needle*. It is business jargon that many people find tiresome, so it fits meetings and strategy talk but sounds odd in casual conversation. The image is a needle on a gauge that moves only when something really changes.
entries.pattern: (not) move the needle (on something)
examples: The new ads got lots of likes, but they didn't **move the needle** on sales.
If we want to **move the needle** on patient wait times, we need more staff, not another survey.
Skipping one latte a week won't **move the needle** on your retirement savings.

drill.sentence: One more yoga class on the schedule won't {{move the needle}}; the gym needs a real reason for people to join.
drill.hint: a noticeable change in the numbers (gauge image; not *make a dent* or *make a difference*)

entries.related: *make a dent (in something)* — reduce a problem a little; *make a difference* — neutral and general; *a game changer* — something that changes a situation completely.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An easy success that can be achieved soon and shows early progress, often used to build support for a bigger plan.
entries.usage: Common in management, consulting and project planning, often in the plural: *Let's look for some quick wins*. It sounds positive and practical, and new leaders often look for quick wins to earn trust. It is close to *low-hanging fruit*, but it names the result rather than the easy task.
entries.pattern: look for / deliver / get a quick win; quick wins
examples: Updating the waiting-room signs was **a quick win** that patients noticed right away.
As the new principal, she went for **a quick win** by fixing the broken water fountains.
Clearing out the hall closet was **a quick win** that made the whole apartment feel tidier.

drill.sentence: Fixing the slow login page would be {{a quick win}}: two days of work, and every user would notice.
drill.hint: fast, easy success (not *an easy win* or *low-hanging fruit*)

entries.related: *low-hanging fruit* — the easiest tasks to do first; *an early win* — the same idea, stressing timing; *a long game* — the opposite, success that takes time.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The moment or process of passing work, a patient or a responsibility from one person or team to another.
entries.usage: Common in American hospitals, software teams and project work: *a clean handoff*, *handoff notes*. It stresses that nothing important should get lost in the transfer. British English more often says *handover*, and the verb is *hand off* (*She handed off the project to Sam*).
entries.pattern: a (smooth / clean) handoff (to someone); hand something off to someone
examples: Many medication errors happen during **handoffs** between shifts, when information gets lost.
Before you go on leave, write up **handoff** notes so Kevin knows where everything stands.
The **handoff** from the old agency to the new one was messy, and some client emails were lost.

drill.sentence: When Rosa left the lab, her {{handoff}} was so thorough that I could rerun all her experiments in a day.
drill.hint: the passing-on of her work (American word; not *handover* or *transition*)

entries.related: *handover* — the usual British word; *a transition* — a longer change from one person or system to another; *onboarding* — helping a new person start.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Praise and credit for an achievement, especially when it is given publicly.
entries.usage: Common in American speech, team chats and emails, usually as *Kudos to* + person + *for* + achievement. It is warm and casual, good for public thanks at work, but in formal writing *credit* or *congratulations* fits better. The *-s* is not a plural ending, so avoid *a kudo*; Americans say KOO-dohz, KOO-dohs or KOO-dahs, and British speakers often say KYOO-doss.
entries.pattern: kudos to someone (for something); deserve kudos
examples: **Kudos to** the night shift for handling three emergencies without a single mistake.
Big **kudos to** my sister for running her first marathon at fifty.
The city deserves **kudos** for finally fixing the potholes on Main Street.

drill.sentence: {{Kudos}} to the whole IT team for getting the system back online in under an hour!
drill.hint: informal praise word from Greek (not *props*, *congrats*, *thanks* or *shout-out*)

entries.related: *props (to someone)* — slang, very casual; *hats off to someone* — I admire what they did; *a shout-out* — a public mention or thanks.
